solution:
[Textbook misprint: the question names FIVE elements and prints only FOUR electronegativity values. The missing value is the one for carbon, which Table 7.5 of this same chapter gives as 2.5; the four printed numbers 1.0, 2.0, 1.5 and 3.0 are the Table 7.5 values for Li, B, Be and N respectively. The stem is transcribed exactly as printed and the answer works from Table 7.5.]

All five elements belong to the SECOND PERIOD, and in order of increasing atomic number they run \(\mathrm{Li}\) (3), \(\mathrm{Be}\) (4), \(\mathrm{B}\) (5), \(\mathrm{C}\) (6), \(\mathrm{N}\) (7). Section 7.5.2(e) explains the trend: electronegativity increases as we move across a period, because the effective nuclear charge increases steadily across the period while the shielding by the core \(1s^2\) electrons stays the same, so the nucleus of the later element pulls a shared electron pair towards itself more strongly. Table 7.5 of this chapter gives the Pauling values in periodic-table order: \(\mathrm{Li}\) 1.0, \(\mathrm{Be}\) 1.5, \(\mathrm{B}\) 2.0, \(\mathrm{C}\) 2.5, \(\mathrm{N}\) 3.0 — a steady rise from left to right.

The question lists the elements OUT of that order, as \(\mathrm{Li}\), \(\mathrm{B}\), \(\mathrm{C}\), \(\mathrm{Be}\), \(\mathrm{N}\), which is why the four printed numbers 1.0, 2.0, 1.5, 3.0 do not look like a rising sequence. Matched to the elements in the order printed they are \(\mathrm{Li}\) 1.0, \(\mathrm{B}\) 2.0, \(\mathrm{C}\) (value not printed — Table 7.5 gives 2.5), \(\mathrm{Be}\) 1.5, \(\mathrm{N}\) 3.0. So each value is exactly the Table 7.5 value for that element, and the apparent irregularity is only the order of listing, not a break in the periodic trend.

\(\mathrm{Cl}\), \(\mathrm{Br}\) and \(\mathrm{I}\) all belong to GROUP 17, and going DOWN that group the order is \(\mathrm{Cl}\) (period 3), \(\mathrm{Br}\) (period 4), \(\mathrm{I}\) (period 5). Section 7.5.2(a) gives the reason for the trend: as we move down a group a new, larger valence shell is added, so the number of core electrons increases and the shielding effect increases, while the effective nuclear charge felt by the valence electrons decreases (section 7.5.1). The valence electrons are therefore held by a weaker attractive force and the atomic radius increases down a group.

The printed values are exactly the entries of Table 7.2 of this chapter — \(\mathrm{Cl}\) 99 pm, \(\mathrm{Br}\) 114 pm, \(\mathrm{I}\) 133 pm — and in group order they read \(99 < 114 < 133\) pm, i.e. the radius rises steadily down group 17. As in the previous question, the numbers look out of sequence only because the question lists the elements as \(\mathrm{Cl}\), \(\mathrm{I}\), \(\mathrm{Br}\) rather than in the order in which they occur in the group.

\(\mathrm{F^{\ominus}}\) and \(\mathrm{Na^{\oplus}}\) are ISOELECTRONIC: \(\mathrm{F}\) has 9 electrons and gains one to give 10, while \(\mathrm{Na}\) has 11 and loses one to give 10. Section 7.5.2(b) states the rule for such a pair — the radii of isoelectronic species vary according to the ACTUAL NUCLEAR CHARGE, and a larger nuclear charge exerts greater attraction on the same set of electrons, so the radius of that species becomes smaller.

Here the nuclear charge of \(\mathrm{F^{\ominus}}\) is \(+9\) and that of \(\mathrm{Na^{\oplus}}\) is \(+11\). The same 10 electrons are therefore pulled in more tightly in \(\mathrm{Na^{\oplus}}\), which is why its radius, 98 pm, is smaller than the 133 pm of \(\mathrm{F^{\ominus}}\). This chapter uses exactly this pair and these two values as its worked illustration of the rule. The result is also consistent with the two general statements in the same section: an anion is larger than the atom it comes from (extra electrons increase the mutual repulsion and lower the effective nuclear charge), while a cation is smaller than its parent atom (fewer electrons, less shielding, larger effective nuclear charge).

\({}_{13}\mathrm{Al}\), \({}_{14}\mathrm{Si}\) and \({}_{15}\mathrm{P}\) are three CONSECUTIVE elements of period 3, with outer electronic configurations \(3s^2 3p^1\), \(3s^2 3p^2\) and \(3s^2 3p^3\) respectively (Table 7.1, groups 13, 14 and 15). Section 7.4.2 says the p-block contains all three traditional types of element — the metals on the left, the nonmetals on the right, and the metalloids along the zig-zag line that separates them — and section 7.5.3(b) gives the trend behind that layout: across a period the ionization enthalpy increases, so the metallic character decreases, while the electron gain enthalpy becomes more negative, so the nonmetallic character increases.

Applying that from left to right along period 3: \(\mathrm{Al}\) is the leftmost of the three, has the lowest ionization enthalpy of the three and only three valence electrons, which it can lose to form \(\mathrm{Al^{3\oplus}}\) — the defining behaviour of a metal (good conductor, forms compounds by LOSS of valence electrons). \(\mathrm{P}\) is the rightmost, has five valence electrons and needs only three more for an octet, so it forms compounds by GAIN or sharing of electrons — a nonmetal. \(\mathrm{Si}\) lies between them, exactly on the zig-zag boundary, with four valence electrons — too many to lose easily and too few to gain easily — so it shows properties intermediate between the two and is classed as a metalloid.

Both \(\mathrm{Cu}\) and \(\mathrm{Zn}\) belong to the d-block, and section 7.4.3 makes the colour of an ion depend on ONE structural feature: most d-block elements possess PARTIALLY FILLED inner d-orbitals, and it is that which gives them properties such as variable oxidation state, paramagnetism and the ability to form coloured ions. The same section names the exception explicitly — \(\mathrm{Zn}\), \(\mathrm{Cd}\) and \(\mathrm{Hg}\), with configuration \(ns^2(n-1)d^{10}\) and hence completely filled s- and d-subshells, do NOT show the properties typical of transition metals.

\(\mathrm{Cu}\) (\(Z = 29\)) has the outer configuration \(4s^1 3d^{10}\), so its common ion \(\mathrm{Cu^{2\oplus}}\) is \(3d^9\) — a partially filled d-subshell, which is why copper salts are coloured. \(\mathrm{Zn}\) (\(Z = 30\)) has the outer configuration \(4s^2 3d^{10}\), so \(\mathrm{Zn^{2\oplus}}\) is \(3d^{10}\) — the d-subshell is still completely filled after the two 4s electrons are lost, there is no partially filled d-subshell left, and zinc salts are therefore colourless.

Outer electronic configuration of \(\mathrm{Ge}\): \(4s^2 3d^{10} 4p^2\).

Justification. The PERIOD number is the principal quantum number of the valence shell (section 7.3.1), so period 4 fixes \(n = 4\). Section 7.3 describes how period 4 is built: it begins with the 4s subshell, then the ten elements from \({}_{21}\mathrm{Sc}\) to \({}_{30}\mathrm{Zn}\) fill the 3d subshell, and only after that do the electrons enter 4p for the next six elements, from \({}_{31}\mathrm{Ga} : [\mathrm{Ar}]4s^2 3d^{10} 4p^1\) to \({}_{36}\mathrm{Kr} : [\mathrm{Ar}]4s^2 3d^{10} 4p^6\). \(\mathrm{Ge}\) is the element immediately after \(\mathrm{Ga}\), so it carries one more 4p electron.

The group number confirms it independently: Table 7.1 gives group 14 the general outer configuration \(ns^2 np^2\), so with \(n = 4\) the valence shell must be \(4s^2 4p^2\), i.e. four valence electrons, with the completely filled inner \(3d^{10}\) lying between them.

Outer electronic configuration of \(\mathrm{Po}\): \(6s^2 4f^{14} 5d^{10} 6p^4\).

Justification. Period 6 fixes \(n = 6\) (section 7.3.1, the period number is the principal quantum number of the valence shell). Problem 7.2 of this chapter establishes the filling order for exactly this period: the sixth period has its subshells filled in increasing order of energy as \(6s < 4f < 5d < 6p\), with electron capacities 2, 14, 10 and 6 respectively, which is why it holds \(2 + 14 + 10 + 6 = 32\) elements. So by the time the 6p subshell begins, the 4f and 5d subshells are already complete.

Group 16 fixes how far into 6p the element sits: Table 7.1 gives group 16 the general outer configuration \(ns^2 np^4\), so the valence shell is \(6s^2 6p^4\) — six valence electrons, two short of an octet, which is consistent with section 7.4.2 describing group 16 (the chalcogens) as reactive nonmetals that readily gain two electrons.

Outer electronic configuration of \(\mathrm{Cu}\): \(4s^1 3d^{10}\).

Justification. Period 4 fixes \(n = 4\), and group 11 places \(\mathrm{Cu}\) in the d-block, whose general outer configuration is \(ns^{0-2}(n-1)d^{1-10}\) (section 7.3.3). Counting outwards along period 4 as section 7.3 describes it — 4s filled first, then 3d — the eleventh element of that period would be expected to reach \(4s^2 3d^9\), giving \(2 + 9 = 11\) outer electrons, which matches the group number.

The actual configuration is \(4s^1 3d^{10}\), and section 7.3.3 gives the reason: variations from the simple aufbau order occur because of the extra stability associated with a half-filled and with a FULLY FILLED subshell. The chapter's own worked illustration of this is \(\mathrm{Cr}\) (\(Z = 24\)), whose outer configuration is \(4s^1 3d^5\) instead of \(4s^2 3d^4\) because both subshells are then half-filled. Copper is the fully-filled counterpart of that same effect: shifting one 4s electron into 3d completes the d-subshell. Note that the total is still \(1 + 10 = 11\) outer electrons, so the group number is unchanged.

General outer electronic configuration of the ten elements from \(\mathrm{La}\) to \(\mathrm{Hg}\): \(6s^2 5d^{1-10}\).

Justification. Both elements lie in period 6, so \(n = 6\) (section 7.3.1). They span groups 3 to 12, which section 7.3.3 identifies as the d-block — the ten groups formed by filling the last electron into a d-orbital, with general outer configuration \(ns^{0-2}(n-1)d^{1-10}\). With \(n = 6\) the d-subshell being filled is \((n-1)d = 5d\), and it is filled progressively from \(5d^1\) at group 3 (\(\mathrm{La}\)) to \(5d^{10}\) at group 12 (\(\mathrm{Hg}\)), the ns subshell normally holding its two electrons throughout. That gives \(6s^2 5d^{1-10}\), and the group number of each member is the total number of these outer electrons — 3 for \(6s^2 5d^1\) up to 12 for \(6s^2 5d^{10}\).

Two points worth noting from this chapter itself. First, the ten elements are \(\mathrm{La}\), \(\mathrm{Hf}\), \(\mathrm{Ta}\), \(\mathrm{W}\), \(\mathrm{Re}\), \(\mathrm{Os}\), \(\mathrm{Ir}\), \(\mathrm{Pt}\), \(\mathrm{Au}\), \(\mathrm{Hg}\); the fourteen lanthanoids (\({}_{58}\mathrm{Ce}\) to \({}_{71}\mathrm{Lu}\)) intervene by atomic number but are f-block and are placed separately at the bottom of the table (sections 7.3.3 and 7.4.4), so they are not among the ten. Second, the \(6s^2\) part is not universal: Problem 7.3 of this chapter gives \({}_{79}\mathrm{Au}\) as \(6s^1 5d^{10}\), one of the fully-filled-subshell variations described in section 7.3.3, so written to cover every member of the series the general form is \(6s^{1-2} 5d^{1-10}\).

\(\mathrm{Li}\) (\(Z = 3\), outer configuration \(2s^1\)) and \(\mathrm{F}\) (\(Z = 9\), outer configuration \(2s^2 2p^5\)) both belong to the SECOND PERIOD, so both lose their electron from the same shell (\(n = 2\)) and both are shielded by the same core, \(1s^2\). Section 7.5.2(c) gives the consequence: because the screening stays the same while the actual nuclear charge rises by one at each step, the effective nuclear charge increases steadily across a period, the outer electron is held more tightly, and the first ionization enthalpy therefore increases across the period. Table 7.4 of this chapter tabulates exactly this run for period 2, from 520 \(\mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) at \(\mathrm{Li}\) to 2080 \(\mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) at \(\mathrm{Ne}\), and the two values quoted in the question are its \(\mathrm{Li}\) and \(\mathrm{F}\) entries.

So removing an electron from \(\mathrm{F}\), where the nucleus carries \(+9\) against the same two shielding electrons, costs about three times as much energy as removing one from \(\mathrm{Li}\), where the nucleus carries only \(+3\). The electronic result of the two removals points the same way: \(\mathrm{Li}\) attains the stable \(1s^2\) duplet of helium on losing its single \(2s\) electron, so the loss is easy, whereas \(\mathrm{F}\) is only one electron short of a complete octet and moves further from it by losing an electron, so it has no tendency to do so. Section 7.5.2(c) states the general form of this contrast: the alkali metal displays the lowest first ionization enthalpy of its period and the inert gas the highest.

Section 7.5.1 defines the effect. In a multi-electron atom the positively charged nucleus attracts the electrons around it, but there is also mutual repulsion among the electrons, and the repulsion by the INNER-SHELL electrons is particularly important: it pushes the outer-shell electrons further from the nucleus, so an outer electron is held less tightly and does not experience the full positive charge of the nucleus. This partial cancellation of the nuclear attraction by the inner electrons is called the SCREENING EFFECT (or shielding effect) of the inner/core electrons.

Quantitatively the net charge an outer electron actually experiences is the effective nuclear charge,

\(Z_{\mathrm{eff}} = Z - \sigma\)

where \(\sigma\) is the screening (shielding) constant, whose value depends on the type of orbital the electron occupies. \(Z_{\mathrm{eff}}\) is always lower than the actual nuclear charge \(Z\).

A suitable example from this chapter is group 1. Table 7.3 gives the first ionization enthalpies of \(\mathrm{Li}\), \(\mathrm{Na}\), \(\mathrm{K}\), \(\mathrm{Rb}\), \(\mathrm{Cs}\) as 520, 496, 419, 403 and 374 \(\mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) — falling steadily down the group even though the nuclear charge rises from \(+3\) to \(+55\). Section 7.5.2(c) explains why: down a group a new shell is added, so the number of core electrons increases, the screening they provide increases, and their effect outweighs the increase in nuclear charge. The effective nuclear charge felt by the single \(ns^1\) valence electron therefore falls, and removing it becomes easier. Compare this with a period, where no electron is added to the core, the screening stays the same, and \(Z_{\mathrm{eff}}\) rises steadily instead.

The two ionization enthalpies refer to the two successive steps written in section 7.5.2(c):

\(\mathrm{X(g) \longrightarrow X^{\oplus}(g) + e^{\ominus}}\) ; \(\Delta_i H_1\)

\(\mathrm{X^{\oplus}(g) \longrightarrow X^{2\oplus}(g) + e^{\ominus}}\) ; \(\Delta_i H_2\)

The first electron is pulled away from a NEUTRAL atom; the second is pulled away from a species that already carries a positive charge. That is the reason the chapter itself gives: the second ionization enthalpy is larger than the first because it involves removal of an electron from a positively charged species, which attracts the electron more strongly than a neutral atom does.

It can also be seen from the electron count. After the first electron leaves, the nuclear charge is unchanged but one electron fewer remains, so — exactly as section 7.5.2(b) argues for a cation being smaller than its parent atom — the shielding is reduced and the effective nuclear charge acting on each remaining electron is larger, and the cation is smaller than the atom. The remaining electrons are therefore held closer and more tightly, and more energy must be supplied to remove the next one. Both ionization enthalpies are positive in any case, since energy must always be supplied to knock an electron out of an atom, so \(\Delta_i H_2 > \Delta_i H_1 > 0\).

Because the members of a group share the same GENERAL OUTER ELECTRONIC CONFIGURATION, and it is the outer electrons that take part in chemical change.

Section 7.3.2 states the structural fact: a new shell is added down a group, so the general outer electronic configuration is expected to be — and for groups 1, 2, 3 and 13 to 18 is found to be — the same down the whole group. Table 7.1 shows it directly: group 1 is \(ns^1\) with \({}_{3}\mathrm{Li} : 2s^1\) and \({}_{11}\mathrm{Na} : 3s^1\); group 17 is \(ns^2 np^5\) with \({}_{9}\mathrm{F} : 2s^2 2p^5\) and \({}_{17}\mathrm{Cl} : 3s^2 3p^5\). Only the value of \(n\) changes.

Section 7.5.3 supplies the link to chemistry: the most fundamental chemical property of an element is its combining power, expressed as valency, and chemical reactivity is decided by the ease with which an element loses or gains electrons — that is, by the ionization enthalpy and the electron gain enthalpy, both of which are governed by the outer configuration. Since every member of a group has the same number of valence electrons and the same number needed to reach an octet, all of them form the same kinds of compound. Table 7.6 shows this concretely: valency stays constant down a group, so group 1 gives \(\mathrm{LiH}\), \(\mathrm{NaH}\), \(\mathrm{KH}\) and group 2 gives \(\mathrm{BeH_2}\), \(\mathrm{MgH_2}\), \(\mathrm{CaH_2}\). The properties are similar rather than identical because \(n\) differs, and with it the atomic size and the effective nuclear charge, so the reactivity varies gradually down the group.

ELECTRONEGATIVITY (section 7.5.2(e)). When two atoms of different elements form a covalent bond the electron pair is shared unequally; the ability of a covalently bonded atom to attract the shared electrons towards itself is called its electronegativity. It depends on the effective nuclear charge experienced by the electron involved in the bond, so it increases across a period and decreases down a group. It is a comparative number on an arbitrary scale rather than a physical quantity with units: Linus Pauling assigned the value 4.0 to fluorine, the element expected to have the highest value, and fixed the rest relative to it (Table 7.5).

ELECTRON GAIN ENTHALPY (section 7.5.2(d)). Addition of an electron to a neutral gaseous atom \(\mathrm{X}\) gives the anion \(\mathrm{X^{\ominus}}\):

\(\mathrm{X(g) + e^{\ominus} \longrightarrow X^{\ominus}(g)}\) ; \(\Delta_{eg}H\)

The enthalpy change that takes place when an electron is added to an isolated gaseous atom in its ground state is the electron gain enthalpy, \(\Delta_{eg}H\). It is a quantitative measure of the ease with which an atom accepts an electron and is expressed in \(\mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\); it may be negative or positive according as the addition is exothermic or endothermic.

WHICH CAN BE MEASURED EXPERIMENTALLY? The electron gain enthalpy. It is the enthalpy change of a definite chemical process and therefore has real units and a measurable value. Section 7.5.2(e) says of the other one in so many words that electronegativity is NOT an experimentally measurable quantity — which is exactly why several different numerical scales of it were devised by different workers, and why Pauling had to fix his scale by assigning a value to fluorine arbitrarily.

**a. \(1s^2\)** — this is \({}_{2}\mathrm{He}\). Section 7.3 notes that the first shell can hold only two electrons, so the first period contains just two elements, \(\mathrm{H} : 1s^1\) and \(\mathrm{He} : 1s^2\), and ends at \(\mathrm{He}\) because \(\mathrm{He}\) has a complete duplet. Problem 7.3 of this chapter works the placement out in full: \(n = 1\) puts it in PERIOD 1, and because its valence shell is completely filled — like the complete octets of the other members of group 18 — it is placed at the end of period 1 in GROUP 18, the inert gases.

**b. \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6\)** — this is \({}_{10}\mathrm{Ne}\). Its outermost shell is \(n = 2\), so it belongs to PERIOD 2, and section 7.3 states that the second period ends with \(\mathrm{Ne}\), which has 8 electrons in its outermost shell and hence a complete octet. Its outer configuration \(2s^2 2p^6\) is the \(ns^2 np^6\) entry of Table 7.1, so it belongs to GROUP 18.

Both elements are therefore inert gases of group 18, differing only in the period, and both are placed in the p-block — \(\mathrm{Ne}\) because its last electron enters a p-subshell, and \(\mathrm{He}\) by the special convention explained in section 7.3.3, since \(\mathrm{He}\) has no p-subshell at all but its completely filled valence shell puts it with the rest of group 18.

**a. \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) is larger than \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\).** Both come from the same atom, \({}_{26}\mathrm{Fe}\), so the nuclear charge is identical at \(+26\); only the electron count differs, \(26 - 2 = 24\) electrons in \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) against \(26 - 3 = 23\) in \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\). Section 7.5.2(b) gives the rule for exactly this situation: a cation is smaller than the atom it is formed from because it contains fewer electrons while the nuclear charge is unchanged, so the shielding effect is less and the effective nuclear charge is larger within the cation. Removing the third electron applies that argument once more, so the remaining electrons of \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) are pulled in more tightly and the higher-charged cation is the smaller one.

**b. \(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}\) is larger than \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\).** \(\mathrm{Mg}\) (period 3) and \(\mathrm{Ca}\) (period 4) both belong to group 2, and section 7.5.2(b) states that ionic radii show the same trends as atomic radii — which, by section 7.5.2(a), increase down a group, because a new larger valence shell is added, the shielding by the extra core electrons increases and the effective nuclear charge felt by the outer electrons falls. Both ions carry the same \(2+\) charge, so the comparison is decided purely by that group trend, and the ion of the element lower in the group is the larger.

**a. \(\mathrm{Li^+}\) is the smaller ion.** \(\mathrm{Li}\) and \(\mathrm{K}\) both belong to group 1, with \(\mathrm{Li}\) in period 2 and \(\mathrm{K}\) in period 4. Section 7.5.2(b) states that ionic radii show the same trends as atomic radii, and section 7.5.2(a) gives that trend down a group: the radius INCREASES, because a new larger valence shell is added, the shielding by the extra core electrons increases and the effective nuclear charge felt by the outer electrons decreases. Table 7.2 measures it for the parent atoms of this very group — \(\mathrm{Li}\) 152 pm against \(\mathrm{K}\) 231 pm. Both ions carry the same \(+1\) charge and are formed by losing the single \(ns^1\) electron, so the comparison is decided purely by that group trend, and the ion of the element higher in the group is the smaller.

**b. \(\mathrm{F^-}\) is the smaller ion.** \(\mathrm{N^{3-}}\) has \(7 + 3 = 10\) electrons and \(\mathrm{F^-}\) has \(9 + 1 = 10\), so the two are ISOELECTRONIC — the case section 7.5.2(b) singles out. For such a pair the radii vary according to the ACTUAL NUCLEAR CHARGE, and a larger nuclear charge exerts greater attraction on the same set of electrons, so that species is the smaller. Here the nuclear charge is \(+7\) for \(\mathrm{N^{3-}}\) and \(+9\) for \(\mathrm{F^-}\), so the ten electrons are drawn in more tightly around fluorine. This is the same argument the chapter applies to \(\mathrm{F^{\ominus}}\) (133 pm) and \(\mathrm{Na^{\oplus}}\) (98 pm), which are also isoelectronic at 10 electrons, with the higher nuclear charge again giving the smaller radius.

**a. Sulfur has the smaller ionization enthalpy.** The diagram places \(\mathrm{O}\) and \(\mathrm{S}\) one below the other in the same group (group 16), with \(\mathrm{O}\) in period 2 and \(\mathrm{S}\) in period 3. Section 7.5.2(c) states that on moving down a group the first ionization enthalpy decreases, because the electron has to be removed from a larger valence shell, the screening due to the core electrons goes on increasing and the effective nuclear charge decreases, so the removal of the outer electron becomes easier. Table 7.3 shows the same fall measured down group 1, from 520 \(\mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) at \(\mathrm{Li}\) to 374 \(\mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) at \(\mathrm{Cs}\). Since \(\mathrm{S}\) lies below \(\mathrm{O}\), \(\mathrm{S}\) is the one from which an electron is more easily removed.

**b. Because of the number of valence electrons each has to lose to reach an inert-gas configuration.** The diagram places \(\mathrm{Li}\) in group 1 and \(\mathrm{Be}\) in group 2, the two s-block groups on the extreme left. By Table 7.1 the outer configuration of \(\mathrm{Li}\) is \(2s^1\) and that of \(\mathrm{Be}\) is \(2s^2\). Section 7.4.1 says s-block elements have only one or two valence electrons which they can lose readily, forming \(\mathrm{M^{\oplus}}\) or \(\mathrm{M^{2\oplus}}\) ions, because their ionization enthalpies are low. \(\mathrm{Li}\) has one such electron, and losing it leaves the stable \(1s^2\) duplet of helium, so it forms \(\mathrm{Li^{\oplus}}\), a \(+1\) ion. \(\mathrm{Be}\) has two, and it must lose both to reach the same \(1s^2\) duplet, so it forms \(\mathrm{Be^{2\oplus}}\), a \(+2\) ion.

**a. Ionic radius.** An atom forms a cation on losing one or more electrons and an anion on gaining one or more. Section 7.5.2(b) defines the ionic radius operationally, the way it is actually obtained: measurements of the distances between neighbouring cations and anions in ionic crystals are used to estimate ionic radii, so the ionic radius is the share of that internuclear distance attributed to the ion concerned. It follows the same trends as the atomic radius — increasing down a group and decreasing across a period. Two consequences stated in the same section are worth attaching to the definition: a cation is SMALLER than the atom it is formed from, because it has fewer electrons for the same nuclear charge, so the shielding is less and the effective nuclear charge larger; and an anion is LARGER than its parent atom, because the extra electrons increase the mutual repulsion and lower the effective nuclear charge.

**b. Electronegativity.** Section 7.5.2(e) defines it as the ability of a covalently bonded atom to attract the shared electron pair towards itself. When two atoms of different elements form a covalent bond the pair is shared unequally, and electronegativity measures which of the two pulls harder. It depends on the effective nuclear charge experienced by the bonding electron, so it increases across a period and decreases down a group. It is not an experimentally measurable quantity; the values in Table 7.5 are on the Pauling scale, on which fluorine was assigned 4.0 and the other elements fixed relative to it.

Section 7.5.3(b) and 7.5.3(c) of this chapter contrast the two classes as follows.

| Property | Metals | Non-metals |
|---|---|---|
| Position in the table | left of the zig-zag line | right of the zig-zag line |
| Electrical conductivity | good conductors | poor conductors |
| How they form compounds | by LOSS of valence electrons | by GAIN of valence electrons in the valence shell |
| Ionization enthalpy | low, so they part with electrons readily | high, so they do not lose electrons |
| Electron gain enthalpy | small or positive | large negative, especially group 17 |
| Ion formed | cations, \(\mathrm{M^{\oplus}}\), \(\mathrm{M^{2\oplus}}\) | anions, \(\mathrm{X^{\ominus}}\), \(\mathrm{X^{2\ominus}}\) |
| Nature of the oxide | basic, e.g. \(\mathrm{Na_2O}\), giving a strong base with water | acidic, e.g. \(\mathrm{Cl_2O_7}\), giving a strong acid with water |

The underlying reason is the same in every row. Chemical reactivity is decided by how easily an element reaches the electronic configuration of the nearest inert gas (section 7.5.3(c)). A metal has few valence electrons and a low ionization enthalpy, so it gets there by LOSING them; a non-metal is only one or two short of an octet and has a highly negative electron gain enthalpy, so it gets there by GAINING them. Hence metals react with oxygen to give basic oxides such as \(\mathrm{Na_2O}\), which reacts with water to give the strong base \(\mathrm{NaOH}\), while non-metals give acidic oxides such as \(\mathrm{Cl_2O_7}\), which reacts with water to give the strong acid \(\mathrm{HClO_4}\). The elements at the centre of the main group are intermediate, and their oxides are amphoteric (for example \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\)), neutral (\(\mathrm{CO}\), \(\mathrm{NO}\)) or weakly acidic (\(\mathrm{CO_2}\)).

[Textbook note (not an error): the identity \(\text{number of valence electrons} = \text{group number}\) holds exactly for the s-block groups 1 and 2 under the IUPAC 1-to-18 numbering this chapter uses, but NOT for the p-block — the chapter's own Table 7.6 gives groups 13 to 18 as 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8 valence electrons, i.e. group number minus 10. The claim as worded is true under the older group I-to-VIII numbering.]

VALENCE ELECTRONS are the electrons in the outermost (valence) shell of an atom — the ones described in section 7.5.3 as deciding the combining power of the element, since chemical reactivity is governed by the ease with which those electrons are lost or gained, and the valency of a main group element is usually equal to the number of them or to the difference between 8 and that number.

Taking the general outer configurations from Table 7.1 and the counts from Table 7.6:

| Group | General outer configuration | Number of valence electrons |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | \(ns^1\) | 1 |
| 2 | \(ns^2\) | 2 |
| 13 | \(ns^2 np^1\) | 3 |
| 14 | \(ns^2 np^2\) | 4 |
| 15 | \(ns^2 np^3\) | 5 |
| 16 | \(ns^2 np^4\) | 6 |
| 17 | \(ns^2 np^5\) | 7 |
| 18 | \(ns^2 np^6\) | 8 |

For the s-block the count IS the group number exactly: group 1 has \(ns^1\), one valence electron (\({}_{3}\mathrm{Li} : 2s^1\), \({}_{11}\mathrm{Na} : 3s^1\)), and group 2 has \(ns^2\), two (\({}_{4}\mathrm{Be} : 2s^2\), \({}_{12}\mathrm{Mg} : 3s^2\)).

For the p-block the count is the GROUP NUMBER MINUS 10 under the IUPAC 1-to-18 numbering used throughout this chapter: group 13 has 3 valence electrons, group 14 has 4, and so on to group 18 with 8, as the table above shows. The subtraction of 10 is simply the ten d-block groups (3 to 12) that lie between the s- and p-blocks and are skipped over in periods 2 and 3. Under the older numbering, in which the p-block groups were labelled III to VIII, the identity "number of valence electrons = group number" held for the p-block as well, and that is the form the question is quoting.

DEFINITION (section 7.5.2(c)). The energy required to remove an electron from an isolated gaseous atom in its ground state is called the ionization enthalpy, \(\Delta_i H\). It is the quantitative measure of the tendency of an element to LOSE an electron and is expressed in \(\mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\):

\(\mathrm{X(g) \longrightarrow X^{\oplus}(g) + e^{\ominus}}\) ; \(\Delta_i H_1\)

It is always positive, since energy must always be supplied to knock an electron out of an atom. Because electrons are lost one at a time, an element has a first, a second and further ionization enthalpies, each larger than the one before.

FACTORS ON WHICH IT DEPENDS, as this chapter uses them:

1. Size of the valence shell / atomic radius — the further the outer electron is from the nucleus, the more easily it is removed.
2. Effective nuclear charge, \(Z_{\mathrm{eff}} = Z - \sigma\) — the greater it is, the more tightly the electron is held.
3. Screening (shielding) by the core electrons — more core electrons mean a smaller \(Z_{\mathrm{eff}}\) and a lower ionization enthalpy (section 7.5.1).
4. The type of orbital the electron occupies — a 2p electron is less penetrating than a 2s electron and so is easier to remove, which is why \(\mathrm{B}\) (801) has a lower value than \(\mathrm{Be}\) (899) in Table 7.4.
5. Electron pairing in an orbital — an electron in a doubly occupied p orbital is easier to remove because of the electron-electron repulsion, which is why \(\mathrm{O}\) (1314) has a lower value than \(\mathrm{N}\) (1402).

VARIATION DOWN A GROUP: it DECREASES. Down a group the electron must be removed from a larger valence shell, the screening by the core electrons increases, and the effective nuclear charge falls, so removal becomes easier. Table 7.3 measures this for group 1: 520, 496, 419, 403, 374 \(\mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) for \(\mathrm{Li}\), \(\mathrm{Na}\), \(\mathrm{K}\), \(\mathrm{Rb}\), \(\mathrm{Cs}\).

VARIATION ACROSS A PERIOD: it INCREASES overall. Across a period no electron is added to the core, so the screening stays the same while the nuclear charge rises by one at each step; \(Z_{\mathrm{eff}}\) therefore increases and the outer electron is held more tightly. Table 7.4 measures this for period 2, rising from 520 \(\mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) at \(\mathrm{Li}\) to 2080 \(\mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) at \(\mathrm{Ne}\) — the alkali metal lowest, the inert gas highest — with the two dips at \(\mathrm{B}\) and \(\mathrm{O}\) explained by factors 4 and 5 above.

ACROSS A PERIOD the atomic size DECREASES. Section 7.5.2(a) gives the reason: as we move across a period the screening caused by the core electrons remains the same, because the added electron enters the same valence shell and nothing is added to the core, while the actual nuclear charge rises by one at each step. The effective nuclear charge therefore goes on increasing, the valence electrons are more tightly bound, and the radius falls. Example, from Table 7.2 for period 2: \(\mathrm{Li}\) 152, \(\mathrm{Be}\) 111, \(\mathrm{B}\) 88, \(\mathrm{C}\) 77, \(\mathrm{N}\) 74, \(\mathrm{O}\) 66, \(\mathrm{F}\) 64 pm — a fall of more than half from one end of the period to the other. The same section notes the trend holds up to group 17.

DOWN A GROUP the atomic size INCREASES. Here a new, larger valence shell is added, so there is an extra shell in the core; the shielding by the increased number of core electrons outweighs the increase in nuclear charge, the effective nuclear charge felt by the outer electrons decreases, and they are held by a weaker attractive force. Example, from Table 7.2 for group 1: \(\mathrm{Li}\) 152, \(\mathrm{Na}\) 186, \(\mathrm{K}\) 231, \(\mathrm{Rb}\) 244, \(\mathrm{Cs}\) 262 pm.

The radius itself is defined in section 7.5.2(a) as one half of the internuclear distance between two adjacent atoms of a metal (metallic radius) or between two single-bonded atoms of a non-metal (covalent radius) — for instance the \(\mathrm{Cl-Cl}\) bond length in \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) is 198 pm, so the atomic radius of \(\mathrm{Cl}\) is 99 pm. The atom has no definite boundary of its own, since the quantum mechanical model describes the extranuclear part as an electron cloud, which is why the size has to be estimated from internuclear distances in this way.

**a. Alkali metals have low ionization enthalpies.** An alkali metal is a group 1 element with the outer configuration \(ns^1\) (Table 7.1) — a single valence electron in the outermost shell, shielded from the nucleus by a complete inner core, so the effective nuclear charge acting on it is small (section 7.5.1). It is also the leftmost element of its period and therefore the largest, so that electron is the furthest from the nucleus: Table 7.2 gives \(\mathrm{Li}\) 152 pm against \(\mathrm{F}\) 64 pm in the same period. On top of that, losing the one electron leaves the stable inert-gas configuration of the preceding noble gas. Section 7.5.2(c) records the measured result — the alkali metal displays the lowest first ionization enthalpy of its period.

**b. Inert gases have exceptionally high ionization enthalpies.** A noble gas has a completely filled valence shell — a complete octet, or a complete duplet in the case of \(\mathrm{He}\) — which section 7.4.2 gives as the reason for their very low chemical reactivity. It is also the LAST element of its period, so having gained a unit of nuclear charge at every step with no increase in core shielding, it has the largest effective nuclear charge and the smallest radius of the period (section 7.5.2(c)). Removing an electron would therefore both cost the most energy and destroy a closed shell, so the value is the highest of the period: Table 7.4 gives \(\mathrm{Ne}\) 2080 \(\mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) against \(\mathrm{Li}\) 520.

**c. Fluorine has less electron affinity than chlorine.** This chapter does not explain this particular case, and it should be noted that its own stated trend points the other way: section 7.5.2(d) says the electron gain enthalpy becomes LESS negative down a group, which taken alone would make \(\mathrm{F}\) the more negative of the two. What the chapter does say is that the trends for electron gain enthalpy are less regular than those for ionization enthalpy, so exceptions to the group trend are to be expected. The accepted reason, which goes beyond what this chapter states, is size: \(\mathrm{F}\) is a very small atom (64 pm, Table 7.2) whose incoming electron has to enter a compact 2p subshell that is already crowded, so a large part of the energy released by the nuclear attraction is cancelled by the extra electron-electron repulsion. In \(\mathrm{Cl}\) (99 pm) the 3p subshell is roomier, the added electron suffers less repulsion, and more energy is released overall — so \(\mathrm{Cl}\), not \(\mathrm{F}\), has the most negative electron gain enthalpy in group 17.

**d. Noble gases possess relatively large atomic size.** Again this chapter does not give the reason directly, but it flags the point: section 7.5.2(a) states the decrease of atomic radius across a period only "upto group 17", and Table 7.2 stops at group 17 with no group 18 column at all — the noble gases are deliberately left outside the trend. The reason, which goes beyond this chapter, follows from the chapter's own DEFINITION of atomic radius as one half of the internuclear distance between two single-bonded atoms of a non-metal or two adjacent atoms of a metal. A noble gas forms neither bond, so no covalent or metallic radius can be measured for it; the value quoted for it is instead a van der Waals radius, taken from the distance between neighbouring atoms that are merely touching and not bonded. That distance is inherently larger than a bond length, so the noble-gas figures appear large and are not comparable with the covalent radii of the elements beside them.

Section 7.5.3(c) links the nature of an oxide to the position of the element in the periodic table: the reactive elements on the extreme left (the alkali metals) form oxides such as \(\mathrm{Na_2O}\) which react with water to give strong bases such as \(\mathrm{NaOH}\); the reactive elements on the right (the halogens) form oxides such as \(\mathrm{Cl_2O_7}\) which react with water to give strong acids such as \(\mathrm{HClO_4}\); and the oxides of the elements in the centre of the main group are amphoteric (for example \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\)), neutral (\(\mathrm{CO}\), \(\mathrm{NO}\)) or weakly acidic (\(\mathrm{CO_2}\)). So basic character follows metallic character, and acidic character follows non-metallic character.

**a. \(\mathrm{Li_2O}\) is the most basic.** \(\mathrm{Li}\) is a group 1 alkali metal, the leftmost of the three elements concerned and the most metallic; Table 7.5 gives it the lowest electronegativity of the three, 1.0. Its oxide is the ionic, basic one, exactly as \(\mathrm{Na_2O}\) is in the chapter's own example, and Problem 7.9 shows that behaviour explicitly — \(\mathrm{Na_2O}\) reacts with acid to give salt and water and does not react with alkali.

**b. \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) is the most acidic.** Of \(\mathrm{Li}\), \(\mathrm{B}\) and \(\mathrm{C}\), carbon lies furthest to the right in period 2 and is the most non-metallic; Table 7.5 gives the electronegativities as \(\mathrm{Li}\) 1.0, \(\mathrm{B}\) 2.0, \(\mathrm{C}\) 2.5, so carbon is the highest of the three. \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) is also the one the chapter itself names as acidic (weakly acidic) among the main group oxides, whereas \(\mathrm{B_2O_3}\), formed by a metalloid of intermediate electronegativity, is the less acidic of the two.

**c. An amphoteric oxide: \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\).** This is the chapter's own example of an amphoteric oxide, and Problem 7.9 demonstrates it with both reactions:

\(\mathrm{Al_2O_3 + 6HCl \longrightarrow 2AlCl_3 + 3H_2O}\)

\(\mathrm{Al_2O_3 + 2NaOH \longrightarrow 2NaAlO_2 + H_2O}\)

Because it reacts with an acid AND with a base to give a salt and water it is amphoteric, which fits the position of \(\mathrm{Al}\) at the centre of the main group elements.
